It grieved me to hear Jim talk that way; it brought him down so. My conscience commenced worrying me worse than ever, till finally I told it, “Quit tormenting me—there’s time yet—I’ll paddle in to the first light and tell on him.” Straight off I felt comfortable and happy and light as a feather. Every trouble had left me. I began watching mighty close for a light, and humming a little to myself. After a while one appeared. Jim hollers:

“We’s safe now, Huck, we’s safe! Get up an’ knock yo’ heels together! Dat’s good ole Cairo at las’, I knows it is!”

I says:

“I’ll go in the canoe and find out, Jim. You know, it might not be.”

He sprang up and made the canoe ready, laid his old coat in the bottom for me to sit on, and handed me the paddle. While I pushed away he says:

“Soon I’ll be hollerin’ for joy, an’ I’ll say it’s all along o’ Huck. I’s a free man, an’ I never could ’a’ been free ’thout Huck; Huck’s done it. Jim ain’t never goin’ to forget you, Huck. You’s de best friend Jim ever had, an’ now you’s de only friend ole Jim’s got.”

I was paddling away, sweating with eagerness to tell on him; but that speech seemed to take all the strength out of me. I moved along slowly after that, and I wasn’t altogether sure whether I was pleased I’d started or sorry. When I got fifty yards away, Jim calls:

“Dere goes faithful ole Huck; de only white gentleman what ever stood by his word to ole Jim.”

Well, it made me feel downright sick. But I says to myself, I’ve got to do it—there’s no getting around it. Just then a skiff came along with two men carrying guns, and they halted and so did I. One says:

“What’s that over there?”

“Part of a raft,” says I.

“You belong aboard it?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Anybody on it?”

“Just one man, sir.”

“Well, five niggers escaped up yonder tonight, above the head of the bend. Is that man of yours black or white?”

I didn’t give an answer at once. I made an effort, but no words would come out. For a second or two I tried to gather my courage and say it, but I wasn’t man enough—didn’t have a rabbit’s pluck. I saw myself giving way, so I quit trying and came out with:

“He’s white.”

“Guess we’ll go look for ourselves.”

“I wish you would,” I says, “because it’s pap aboard there, and maybe you could help me pull the raft to shore over by that light.

Whilst these events were taking place at the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in his former den—the very one from which the girl had taken Oliver—pondering beside a dim and smoky fire. Across his knee lay a pair of bellows, with which he had seemingly been attempting to encourage a livelier blaze; but profound reflection had overtaken him. Folding his arms upon them and supporting his chin on his thumbs, he stared absently at the rusted bars.

Behind him, at a table, the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling were absorbed in whist, the Artful playing dummy against the other two. The first gentleman’s face, remarkably intelligent on every occasion, gained a particular interest from his scrupulous attention to the game and his careful study of Mr. Chitling’s hand. Upon this, whenever opportunity allowed, he directed various searching looks, prudently adjusting his own play according to what his neighbour’s cards revealed. The night was cold, and the Dodger kept his hat on, as was indeed frequently his practice indoors. A clay pipe also rested between his teeth; he removed it only momentarily when he thought fit to seek refreshment from a quart pot standing on the table, filled with gin-and-water for the company’s convenience.

Master Bates likewise attended to the cards; yet his disposition being more excitable than that of his accomplished companion, he resorted rather more often to the gin-and-water. He further permitted himself numerous jokes and observations unrelated to the business in hand, all singularly inappropriate to a scientific rubber. Indeed, the Artful, relying upon their intimate friendship, took several opportunities to remonstrate solemnly with his partner in acquaintance over these lapses. Master Bates accepted every reproof with perfect good humour, merely inviting his friend to be “blowed,” suggesting that he put his head into a sack, or producing another elegantly phrased pleasantry of much the same character. The felicity of these replies aroused great admiration in Mr. Chitling. It was noteworthy that this latter gentleman and his partner lost without exception; and that, instead of vexing Master Bates, their misfortune seemed to give him the liveliest pleasure. He burst into tremendous laughter whenever a deal ended, declaring he had never, in the whole course of his existence, witnessed so jolly a game.

“That makes two doubles and the rubber,” said Mr. Chitling, his face much lengthened, drawing half-a-crown out of his waistcoat pocket. “Never did I see a chap like you, Jack; everything comes your way.”

‘Well, monsieur le mauvais sujet,’ exclaimed the old lady when he came into the room, ‘why have you stayed away from me so long?’

‘My dear Lady Clem, I haven’t a moment of my own,’ Lord Arthur answered with a smile.

‘You mean, I suppose, that you spend the whole day roaming about with Miss Sybil Merton, purchasing chiffons and talking absurdities? I cannot see why marriage should occasion such a commotion. In my young days we never thought of billing and cooing before other people—or by ourselves, for that matter.’

‘I assure you, Lady Clem, I haven’t set eyes on Sybil for twenty-four hours. So far as I can discover, her milliners have entire possession of her.’

‘Naturally; that alone brings you to an ugly old woman like me. I wonder men never learn their lesson. On a fait des folies pour moi, and look at me now, a miserable rheumatic thing with a false front and an ill temper. Indeed, without dear Lady Jansen, who supplies me with the worst French novels she can discover, I doubt whether I could endure the day. Doctors serve no purpose except to extract their fees. They cannot so much as cure my heartburn.’

‘I have brought something to cure that, Lady Clem,’ said Lord Arthur solemnly. ‘A marvellous invention of an American’s.’

‘I don’t believe I care for American inventions, Arthur. In fact, I am sure I don’t. I have recently read some American novels, and found them quite ridiculous.’

‘But there is nothing ridiculous in this, Lady Clem! I promise you it is an absolute cure. You must undertake to try it.’ Lord Arthur drew the small box from his pocket and placed it in her hand.

‘The box, at any rate, is delightful, Arthur. Is it truly a gift? How very kind of you. And this is the marvellous remedy? It resembles a bonbon. I shall swallow it immediately.’

‘Good heavens, Lady Clem!’ cried Lord Arthur, seizing her hand. ‘You must do no such thing. The medicine is homoeopathic, and taking it when you haven’t heartburn might cause you endless mischief. Wait for an attack, and take it then. The effect will astonish you.’

‘I should prefer to take it at once,’ said Lady Clementina, lifting the little clear capsule to the light, the bubble of liquid aconitine floating inside. ‘I am certain it tastes delicious. The truth is, although I detest doctors, I adore medicines. Still, I shall save it for the next attack.’

‘And when do you expect that?’ Lord Arthur asked eagerly.
